scenes.title: The next step, accounted for
scenes.text: Hi, I'm Shivam Gupta, and this is Looplight.

scenes.title: 01 / Anita is home. Care is still unfinished.
scenes.text: Anita has just left the hospital. Her daughter Maya has the discharge document. But a result is still pending, another test needs follow-up, and someone needs to track what happens next. Anita and Maya are fictional. The coordination problem is real.

scenes.title: 02 / Every action keeps its source
scenes.text: Looplight turns the instructions in a discharge document into a follow-up ledger. Every confirmed action keeps its source, the person tracking it, and a record of what happened.

scenes.title: 03 / The document starts the plan
scenes.text: Let's follow Anita's example. I open the sample document and run the analysis. A small trained text model works with explicit rules to suggest follow-up items. It runs without a paid model API.

scenes.title: 04 / Review the whole source
scenes.text: The review screen is the important part. I can see the exact sentence behind each suggestion. I review the whole document, including sentences the system did not turn into tasks. I can correct a suggestion or add something it missed.

scenes.title: 05 / Unclear details stay visible
scenes.text: Dates remain connected to the original wording. If the document is unclear, Looplight leaves a question for the care team. It does not invent a clinical deadline.

scenes.title: 06 / A named tracker for the next step
scenes.text: I confirm the follow-up and give Maya responsibility for tracking one action. That records who is following up. It does not mean Maya is the clinician responsible for treatment.

scenes.title: 07 / Receipt and review stay separate
scenes.text: Now a result has arrived. Watch what happens when I record that. The result can be received while clinician review remains outstanding. A file arriving is only one step.

scenes.title: 08 / Record the reported ending
scenes.text: I record the separate report of clinician review and the outcome before closing the loop. The history shows what the user reported, rather than presenting it as independently verified medical evidence.

scenes.title: 09 / A plan people can take with them
scenes.text: The plan can also leave the app. I can print a brief for the next conversation, export calendar reminders, or download the structured record. In a signed-in care space, plans are saved to the account.

scenes.title: 10 / A business hypothesis to test
scenes.text: For the first customer, I would test this with a primary-care or transitions coordinator who already chases discharge follow-up. The initial pricing hypothesis is one hundred and forty-nine dollars per month for one hundred care episodes. The pilot must show whether staff time saved justifies that price.

scenes.title: 11 / A small model with visible limits
scenes.text: This is a working MVP with synthetic evaluation, not a clinically validated product. The model's raw five-category accuracy was eighty-two percent on fifty separate synthetic challenge examples. It abstained on forty-four, so human review remains central.

scenes.title: 12 / A supervised pilot comes next
scenes.text: The next step is a supervised pilot that measures omissions and preparation time. I built Looplight with AI-assisted development. The goal is simple: every next step has a source, a person, and a recorded ending.
